drafts.title: Your Model 3 or Y can now keep the lights on
drafts.angle: First-hand owner take on Tesla's Powershare home backup coming to Model 3/Y. You own a Tesla and solar; say what it means for a house in Grand Junction.
bullets: Tesla: Model 3 and Y ordered after Oct 1, 2026 get Powershare Home Backup (car powers the house in an outage).
Tesla says 2+ days for an average home (~30 kWh/day).
Home backup only for now; it can't send power to the grid yet.
Ask followers: would this change your generator plans?
drafts.body:
The car in my driveway just turned into a backup generator. Sort of.

Tesla says Model 3 and Model Y ordered after October 1 can power your house during an outage. They figure two-plus days for an average home.

No gas can. No pull cord. No noise at 2 AM.

For older folks on oxygen, a fridge full of insulin, or just a freezer full of elk, that matters. [Your take: would you use it? Does your Model Y qualify?]

One catch: it is home backup only right now. The car can't sell power back to the grid yet.

Who here is ditching the generator?

drafts.title: 85,774 homes just helped hold up California's grid
drafts.angle: Quote-post Tesla Energy's record. Plain words: regular homes acting like a power plant, and getting paid.
bullets: 85,774 Powerwall homes sent 601 MW to the grid Tuesday evening (Tesla Energy dashboard).
About 7 kW per house at peak.
Owners get paid through California programs; Tesla paid $9.9M to VPP participants in 2024.
Record broke the old one in under a month.
drafts.body:
85,774 regular homes just did the job of a power plant.

Tuesday evening, California Powerwall owners sent 601 megawatts back to the grid at the same time. That's a new record, and it beat the last one in less than a month.

Nobody built a new plant. Nobody ran a smokestack. Batteries in garages did it, and the owners get paid for it.

[Your take: what would you do with a check from your battery? Do we have anything like this on the Western Slope?]

This is how the grid gets stronger without your bill going up.

drafts.title: 1 in 3 new solar homes now get a battery
drafts.window: Fri ~noon MT (alt to #2, don't twin same day)
drafts.angle: Solar plus battery is becoming normal. Tie to your own solar and the Powerwall as your next chapter.
bullets: Berkeley Lab: 37% of new 2025 home solar systems included a battery, up from 25% in 2024.
Battery stores midday sun for the expensive evening hours.
Many places also pay battery owners during grid events.
drafts.body:
Solar used to mean panels. Now more than 1 in 3 new solar homes add a battery too.

Berkeley Lab looked at about 450,000 systems installed last year. 37% came with a battery, up from 25% the year before.

Why? The sun shines at noon. Families use the most power at suppertime. A battery saves the cheap noon power for the pricey evening.

[Your take: I got solar at 60. Is a battery my next step? What are folks paying?]

If you're pricing solar, ask about a battery from day one.

drafts.title: An AI that calls Mom every morning
drafts.angle: AI for the masses: a real program helping lonely older people. Not scary, just kind.
bullets: New York's Office for the Aging extended its ElliQ AI companion program.
Users talk to it ~48 times a day; 94% say they feel less lonely (program data).
It checks in, nudges walks, reminds them to call family.
drafts.body:
The scariest thing about getting older isn't AI. It's being alone.

New York State has been giving older folks a small AI companion called ElliQ. It says good morning, asks how they slept, reminds them to take a walk or call their daughter.

The state's numbers: people talk to it about 48 times a day, and 94% say they feel less lonely.

It doesn't replace family. It fills the quiet hours in between.

[Your take: would your parents use this? Would you?]

drafts.title: Staying home longer without cameras in every room
drafts.angle: AI keeping older adults independent while respecting privacy. Answers the 'Big Brother' fear head-on.
bullets: Nottingham Trent University built a low-cost system using radar, heat sensors and smart plugs, with AI to spot falls or emergencies.
Goal: help older people stay in their own homes longer.
drafts.body:
Most of us want to grow old in our own house. Most of us also don't want a camera in the bathroom.

Researchers in England built a cheap setup that skips the cameras. It uses heat sensors, a little radar and smart plugs. AI watches the patterns: did the coffee pot come on, is someone moving around? If something looks wrong, like a fall, it alerts family.

That's AI working for us, not watching us.

[Your take: would you put this in a parent's home? Your own?]
